# Operator economics: Latvia-based seller (generated by `models/operator_economics.py`)

EUR; ECB rate 1.1206 USD/EUR (2026-10-09). Sources: Stripe [S104], Paddle [S105], Latvian tax [S100][S099], Enterprise Register [S102]. Simplified illustration: **not tax advice**. Items marked ASSUMPTION are placeholders.

## A. What the seller keeps from one EUR 49 (net) monthly subscription, by customer type and payment route

| Customer | Customer pays | VAT in price | Stripe direct, seller files VAT | + Stripe Tax Basic | Paddle (merchant of record) | Stripe Managed Payments (MoR, LV eligibility unconfirmed) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| EU consumer (B2C), OSS: VAT of customer's country added | €59.29 | €10.29 | €47.86 | €47.56 | €45.59 | €45.79 |
| EU business with VAT ID (B2B): reverse charge, no VAT charged | €49.00 | €0.00 | €48.02 | €48.02 | €46.10 | €46.30 |
| Latvian customer (B2B or B2C): Latvian VAT 21% | €59.29 | €10.29 | €47.86 | €47.56 | €45.59 | €45.79 |
| US business or consumer: outside EU VAT; local US sales-tax rules may apply (not modelled) | €49.00 | €0.00 | €46.23 | €46.23 | €46.10 | €44.51 |
| UK business: outside EU VAT (UK VAT reverse-charge by customer) | €49.00 | €0.00 | €46.55 | €46.55 | €46.10 | €44.83 |

Reading the table (CALCULATION):
- Direct Stripe processing leaves the seller about 94–98% of the net price, depending on card type and currency conversion. A merchant of record (MoR) leaves about 93–94% (Paddle) or 91–95% (Stripe Managed Payments).
- The MoR premium against direct Stripe ranges from about €0.1 (US card with currency conversion) to €2.3 (EU consumer) per €49 sale, i.e. 0–5% of revenue. In exchange, the MoR becomes the seller of record. It registers, collects and files indirect taxes abroad and handles disputes [S105][S104].
- Whether the premium is worth paying depends on the compliance workload it replaces (OSS returns, non-EU registrations, dispute handling). That workload is not quantified here (UNKNOWN; ask an accountant for a quote).
- US state sales tax and other non-EU indirect taxes on digital services are **not modelled**. A MoR handles them, and direct sellers must check them.

## C. From company profit to owner (Latvian CIT on distribution)

| Profit distributed | Standard regime: owner receives | tax | Alternative regime (individual-owned): owner receives | tax | If retained in company |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| €10,000 | €8,000 | €2,000 | €7,990 | €2,010 | €0 CIT until distributed |
| €50,000 | €40,000 | €10,000 | €39,950 | €10,050 | €0 CIT until distributed |
| €100,000 | €80,000 | €20,000 | €79,900 | €20,100 | €0 CIT until distributed |

Under the two regimes as KPMG describes them [S100], the owner's take is almost identical (80.0% vs 79.9% of distributed profit). Ask an accountant what the alternative regime actually changes, such as interaction with the 3% surcharge above €200k or the timing. Retained profit is untaxed, which favours reinvestment (CALCULATION from published rates).

## D. Buying model/API services as an internal agent operator

A USD 2,000/month API bill (≈€1,785) from a non-Latvian provider is a B2B service taxed where the buyer is established (VAT Law s.19(1)). The Latvian buyer self-assesses 21% VAT ≈ €375 under reverse charge (s.88/89 [S099]). For a fully taxable, VAT-registered business this is reported and deducted in the same return, so it is cash-neutral. Under s.59(6), receiving such services removes the €50,000 small-business registration exemption, so even a very small company buying foreign APIs or cloud must be VAT-registered (per the 2024 English translation; confirm against the current text with an adviser). Under the micro-enterprise tax regime, taxpayers must not be VAT payers [S100], so the two rules appear to be in tension for agent businesses buying foreign APIs (INTERPRETATION requiring professional confirmation).
